summary: Marswalk Planner is an interactive map that a Mars astronaut can use to plan and carry out a safe, science-rich surface walk (EVA) in Jezero Crater, the ancient lake explored by NASA's Perseverance rover. It layers live NASA optical, thermal and topographic data down to 25 cm per pixel. On top of that it adds a planned route to four science stops, hazard zones, and a safety engine that gives any route a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO call based on walking time, suit consumables and hazard crossings. Live solar activity data from NASA DONKI drives a shelter advisory, and a helmet HUD mode shows the essentials on the surface. Today's Mars maps are built for regional and global views. Marswalk Planner turns that data into the hyperlocal, safety-first map that one astronaut on one walk needs.
details:
What it does

Marswalk Planner is a mission-planning and on-surface map for a human EVA (Marswalk) in Jezero Crater, the ancient lake explored by NASA's Perseverance rover. It helps an astronaut answer four questions before stepping outside: Where is the science? Where is the ground safe? Can I get back in time? Is it safe from radiation today?

How it works

- Layered NASA data with a toggle and opacity slider for each layer:

- Optical: Viking color mosaic, MRO CTX at 6 m/px, MRO HiRISE at 25 cm/px

- Thermal: Mars Odyssey THEMIS day and night infrared, MGS TES thermal inertia

- Topographic: MGS MOLA + ESA Mars Express HRSC color hillshade

- A habitat near Perseverance's landing site and a planned loop to four science stops:

- Séítah: olivine rock that dates the crater floor

- Máaz: lava altered by water

- The delta front: lake sediments, the best target for biosignatures

- The upper fan: flood-carried boulders

Each stop lists its science objective, supporting data and kit.

- Hazard zones: no-go dune fields where a suit or rover could sink, plus caution zones for a steep scarp and a boulder field.

- A safety engine that works out route distance on Mars's real radius (3,389.5 km), walking time, science time and suit consumables margin, and detects hazard crossings. Every route gets a live GO / CAUTION / NO-GO call. A walk-back ring shows how far the crew can go and still return with a 1-hour reserve.

- Custom routes: click on the map to add waypoints, and the plan is re-checked instantly.

- Live space weather from the NASA DONKI API (solar flares, CMEs and solar particle events) with a SHELTER advisory. Mars has no global magnetic field, so radiation is a key EVA risk.

- Helmet HUD mode: a visor-style display of the next stop, oxygen margin, route and radiation status.

- A self-playing guided tour mode that walks new users through the whole tool.

Benefits and intended impact

NASA's Mars data is rich but scattered across missions and built for global views. Marswalk Planner turns it into one hyperlocal decision tool for one astronaut on one walk, putting crew safety first while getting the most science out of every hour outside. The same approach can be reused for any landing site on Mars, and later for the Moon.

How it is creative

- It reads thermal infrared as a "where can I walk" map: high thermal inertia means solid rock, and low means loose sand.

- It combines science value, terrain hazards, suit consumables and live radiation in a single GO / NO-GO decision.

- The same map works in three settings: planning in the habitat, a tablet in the field, and a helmet heads-up display.

Factors we considered

- Astronaut safety first: hazard zones, a consumables reserve, a walk-back limit and radiation shelter alerts.

- Reduced mobility in a spacesuit: walking speed and time per stop are adjustable.

- Correct Mars geometry: standard web-map tools assume Earth's radius and would overstate Mars distances by about 1.9×, so we wrote our own distance maths.

- Honest data: science-stop locations and hazard boundaries are marked as approximate planning annotations, and space weather is labelled advisory because it is measured from Earth's vicinity.

Tools and technologies

HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Leaflet 1.9.4 (geographic EPSG:4326 projection); NASA/JPL Mars Trek WMTS tile services; the NASA DONKI API; WebAudio and the Web Speech API (guided tour); GitHub and GitHub Pages. No build step: it runs in any modern browser on desktop, tablet or phone.

Future work

Slope maps from HiRISE elevation models, rover-assisted routes, two-person EVA planning, and an AR helmet display.
